title: The First 30 Days in a New Home: Your Maintenance Checklist
description: Moved in recently? Here are the 15 things every new homeowner should do in the first 30 days — before something breaks.

children.text: Why the first 30 days matter most

The first month in a new home is your best window to understand what you own before problems emerge. Sellers disclose what they know, inspectors catch what they can see — but there's a layer of institutional knowledge about your home that only time and attention will reveal. Here's what to do now.
Week 1: Learn your systems
Find every shutoff valve.
Main water shutoff, individual fixture shutoffs under sinks and toilets, gas shutoffs at appliances. Know exactly where they are before you need them urgently at 2am.
Locate your electrical panel.
Label every breaker if they aren't already labeled. This takes 20 minutes and saves enormous confusion later.
Find your HVAC filter.
Check the size printed on the frame, buy three replacements, and put them somewhere obvious. Change it now if you don't know when the previous owner last did.
Test every GFCI outlet.
Press the test button on outlets in bathrooms, kitchen, garage, and exterior. They should click off. Press reset to restore. Any that don't respond need an electrician.
Week 2: Document everything
Photograph every appliance nameplate.

The nameplate on your water heater, HVAC, refrigerator, washer, dryer, and dishwasher tells you the model, serial number, and manufacture date. You'll need this for warranty claims, service calls, and replacement planning.
Note the age of major systems.
Water heater over 10 years old? HVAC over 15? Start budgeting for replacement. Knowing now prevents emergencies later.
Find all warranties and manuals.
Check kitchen drawers, the garage, and any folders left by the previous owner. Scan and upload anything you find.
Week 3: Address immediate maintenance
Change the locks.
You don't know who has a key. This is non-negotiable.
Test smoke and CO detectors.
Replace batteries in all of them regardless of status. If any are over 10 years old, replace the units.
Flush the water heater.
If the previous owner didn't maintain it, there's likely sediment buildup. Connect a hose to the drain valve and let it run for a few minutes.
Check the attic and crawl space.
Look for signs of water intrusion, pest activity, or inadequate insulation. These are the areas most likely to hide problems the inspection missed.
Week 4: Set up your maintenance system
Build your home inventory.
Every appliance, every system, every major component — documented with model, serial number, age, and warranty status. Steadwell's AI nameplate scan does this in seconds per item.
Schedule your first year of maintenance.
HVAC service in fall, gutter cleaning after leaf season, roof inspection annually. Get these on the calendar now while motivation is high.
Find your contractors.
Get recommendations for a plumber, electrician, and HVAC tech before you need them urgently. The best contractors have waitlists; emergency calls go to whoever is available.
Start tracking in Steadwell

title: What Your Home Inspection Didn't Tell You
description: Home inspections catch a lot — but not everything. Here are the most common things inspectors miss and how to find them yourself.

children.text: What a home inspection actually covers

A standard home inspection is a visual examination of accessible areas performed in 2-4 hours. Inspectors are generalists — they identify visible symptoms of potential problems, not underlying causes. They're also limited by what they can see: inside walls, under slabs, and behind finished surfaces are all off-limits.
The most common misses
Roof life remaining.

Inspectors note the condition of shingles they can see, but rarely give you a reliable estimate of remaining life. An inspector might call a roof "functional" when it has 2 years left. Always ask: when was it installed and what material is it?
HVAC efficiency and age.

Inspectors confirm the system turns on. They don't test efficiency, measure refrigerant levels, or flag a 14-year-old unit that's running on borrowed time. Get a dedicated HVAC inspection from an HVAC company if the system is over 10 years old.
Polybutylene plumbing.

Homes built between 1978 and 1995 may have gray plastic "PB" supply pipes that degrade and fail without warning. Inspectors often note it but don't always convey the urgency. Look for gray plastic pipes under sinks and in the utility room.
Sewer line condition.

A standard inspection doesn't include a sewer scope — a camera run through the drain line to check for root intrusion, breaks, or bellying. This is a $150-300 add-on that catches $5,000-15,000 problems. Always get one on homes over 20 years old.
Attic insulation and ventilation.

Inspectors look in the attic but often spend 30 seconds there. Poor insulation and inadequate ventilation cause ice dams, premature roof failure, and high energy bills. Measure your insulation depth — you want R-38 to R-60 in most climates.
Chinese drywall.

Installed in some Florida homes during the 2004-2011 construction boom, it off-gasses sulfur compounds that corrode wiring and smell like rotten eggs. Inspectors are not required to test for it. If your home was built or renovated during this period, ask specifically.
What to do after closing

Even if your inspection was thorough, plan a follow-up specialist inspection for anything the inspector flagged as "monitor" — that's code for "this will be a problem but not today." Address it on your timeline, not in a crisis.
Document what you find

As you discover the real state of your home's systems, log it in Steadwell. Every note you take now becomes part of your home's history — useful when you sell, file an insurance claim, or hire a contractor.

title: How to Build a Home Maintenance Budget (With Real Numbers)
description: How much should you budget for home maintenance? Here's the honest math, the rules of thumb that actually work, and how to build a reserve that protects you.

children.text: The rules of thumb

Financial planners typically recommend budgeting 1-3% of your home's value annually for maintenance and repairs. On a $350,000 home that's $3,500-10,500 per year. The range is wide because it depends heavily on your home's age, condition, and climate.

A better rule: budget 1% for a newer home in good condition, 2% for a home 10-25 years old, and 3%+ for anything older or with deferred maintenance. Florida homeowners should add a hurricane/storm premium regardless of home age.
What the money actually goes to
Routine maintenance (budget monthly):
HVAC filters ($15-30/month), pest control ($50-80/quarter), lawn and landscaping ($100-300/month), gutter cleaning ($150-300/year).
Annual service calls (budget yearly):
HVAC tune-up ($80-150), water heater flush ($0 DIY or $100-150 with plumber), roof inspection ($100-200), dryer vent cleaning ($80-150).
Irregular big-ticket items (budget as reserve):

This is where most homeowners get blindsided. A new roof costs $8,000-25,000. An HVAC system costs $5,000-12,000. A water heater costs $800-1,500. A kitchen appliance costs $500-2,000. These aren't surprises — they're predictable based on age.
The sinking fund approach

The smartest homeowners treat major system replacements like predictable expenses, not emergencies. If your roof is 12 years old and has an 8-year life remaining, you have 8 years to save $15,000 — that's $156/month. If your HVAC is 10 years old and you have 5-8 years left, saving $100/month gives you $6,000-9,600 when you need it. This approach converts emergencies into planned purchases.
What throws budgets off

Deferred maintenance is the biggest budget killer. Every year you skip an HVAC service, roof inspection, or gutter cleaning increases the probability and severity of a larger failure. The $150 you save on an HVAC tune-up can cost $8,000 in premature replacement. Budget for preventive maintenance first — it's the best ROI in homeownership.

title: Florida Homeowner's Guide to Hurricane Season Prep
description: Hurricane season runs June through November. Here's exactly what Florida homeowners should do before, during, and after a storm to protect their home and family.

children.text: When to start preparing

The Atlantic hurricane season officially runs June 1 through November 30, with peak activity August through October. The right time to prepare is before any storm is named or forecast — once a hurricane watch is issued, hardware stores are sold out and contractors are booked. Prepare in May or early June, every year.
Structural and exterior prep
Roof:

Have your roof inspected annually before hurricane season. Make sure all shingles are secured and flashing around penetrations is intact. Loose shingles become projectiles in high winds. If your roof is over 15 years old, get a professional assessment of its wind resistance rating.
Hurricane shutters or impact glass:

If you have shutters, test them now — not when a storm is 48 hours out. Make sure hardware is in place, tracks are clear, and you remember how to install them. If you don't have shutters, plywood is a last resort, not a plan.
Garage door:

The garage door is often the weakest point in a home's envelope. Older doors without horizontal bracing can fail in high winds, which compromises the entire structure. Consider a door brace kit ($150-300) if your door isn't rated for your wind zone.
Trees and landscaping:

Have a certified arborist inspect mature trees within falling distance of your home every 2-3 years. Remove dead branches before the season. Palms are generally fine; oaks and pines with structural issues are the biggest risk.
Systems prep
Generator:

If you have a generator, run it under load for 30 minutes before season to confirm it starts reliably. Check fuel and oil. If you don't have one, a dual-fuel portable generator (runs on gasoline or propane) provides flexibility when gas stations have lines.
Water heater and plumbing:
Know where your main water shutoff is. If flooding is possible, turn off the water supply to protect against backflow contamination.
HVAC:
Clear debris from around the outdoor unit. After a storm, do not run your AC until you've confirmed the unit wasn't submerged or hit by debris — running a damaged compressor destroys it.
Documentation prep

This is where most homeowners fall short. Before hurricane season: photograph every room of your home and every major appliance. Store these photos in the cloud — not just on your phone. If your home is damaged, these photos are the difference between a smooth insurance claim and a disputed one.
Store digital copies of your insurance policy, home inventory, and mortgage documents somewhere accessible off-site or in the cloud. Steadwell's document vault backs up to the cloud automatically.
The 72-hour kit

FEMA recommends 72 hours of supplies minimum, but Florida's post-storm reality often means 7-10 days without power. Stock: water (1 gallon per person per day), non-perishable food, medications (90-day supply if possible), flashlights and batteries, portable chargers, cash, first aid kit, and important documents.

title: How Long Do Home Appliances Last? Lifespan Guide for Every Major Appliance
description: How long should your refrigerator, washer, dishwasher, and HVAC actually last? Here's the definitive lifespan guide with replacement signals for every major home appliance.

children.text: Why appliance age matters

Knowing how old your appliances are — and how long they typically last — is the difference between planning a replacement and experiencing an emergency. A refrigerator that dies on a holiday weekend, a washer that floods the laundry room, or an HVAC that fails in July are all stressful and expensive. Most of these failures are predictable.
Kitchen appliances
Refrigerator:
13-17 years. Signs to watch: excessive condensation, unusual noises, inconsistent temperatures, compressor running constantly, or repairs costing more than 50% of replacement cost.
Dishwasher:
9-12 years. Signs to watch: water not draining, dishes coming out dirty after cleaning the filter, door latch issues, or rust inside the tub.
Oven/range:
15-20 years for gas; 13-15 for electric. Gas ranges last longer because they have fewer electronic components. Signs to watch: uneven heating, burners that won't light, or control board failures.
Microwave:
9-10 years. Built-in over-the-range microwaves tend to last longer than countertop units. Signs to watch: arcing, uneven heating, or door seal damage.
Garbage disposal:
10-12 years. Signs to watch: frequent resets, leaks from the bottom (seal failure), or grinding noise without clearing.
Laundry
Washer:
10-14 years. Front-loaders have shorter lifespans than top-loaders on average. Signs to watch: excessive vibration, water not draining, or error codes that don't clear.
Dryer:
13-15 years. Signs to watch: clothes taking multiple cycles to dry (clean the vent first), excessive heat, or drum not turning.
HVAC and water systems
Central AC:
15-20 years. Florida systems trend toward the lower end due to heavy use. Signs to watch: refrigerant leaks, frozen coils, or rising energy bills without usage changes.
Furnace/heat pump:
15-20 years. Signs to watch: short cycling, uneven heating, yellow burner flame (should be blue), or carbon monoxide detector alarms.
Water heater (tank):
8-12 years. Signs to watch: rust-colored water, rumbling noise, water around the base, or inconsistent hot water.
Water heater (tankless):
20+ years with proper maintenance. Annual descaling is essential in hard-water areas.

title: DIY vs. Hire a Pro: How to Decide for Every Home Repair
description: Not every home repair needs a contractor — but some definitely do. Here's a practical framework for deciding when to DIY and when to call a pro.

children.text: The real cost of DIY

DIY saves money on labor — typically 40-60% of a professional repair cost. But it costs time, requires tools, and carries the risk of doing it wrong. A botched DIY repair can cost more to fix than the original professional quote. The right framework isn't "can I do this?" but "should I do this?"
Always hire a pro
Electrical panel work.
Breaker replacement, panel upgrades, and any work on your main electrical service requires a licensed electrician. The risk of fire and electrocution is not theoretical.
Gas line work.
Any repair or modification to gas supply lines requires a licensed plumber or gas fitter. Gas leaks kill people.
Structural work.
Removing walls, modifying load-bearing elements, or anything that requires a permit needs a licensed contractor and inspection.
Roof replacement.
Working on a steep roof without proper safety equipment and training is one of the leading causes of homeowner fatalities. The savings aren't worth the risk.
HVAC refrigerant work.
Handling refrigerant requires EPA certification. This isn't a legal technicality — refrigerant under pressure is genuinely dangerous.
Good DIY candidates
Painting.
Interior painting is one of the highest-ROI DIY projects. Labor is 70-80% of professional painting costs. With proper prep, results are comparable.
Caulking and weatherstripping.
Straightforward, high-impact, and completely reversible if done imperfectly.
Replacing faucets and fixtures.
With the water supply shut off, most faucet replacements are 30-60 minute jobs requiring only basic tools.
Drywall patching.
Small holes (under 6 inches) are genuinely beginner-friendly with a patch kit from a hardware store.
Appliance maintenance.
Cleaning dryer vents, replacing water heater anode rods, descaling tankless heaters — these are high-value maintenance tasks well within reach of most homeowners.
The permit question

If a project requires a permit, you need a licensed contractor in most jurisdictions. Unpermitted work can void your insurance, create liability when you sell, and result in fines. When in doubt, call your local building department — they'll tell you whether a permit is required before you start.

title: How to Lower Your Homeowner's Insurance Premium Without Reducing Coverage
description: Homeowner's insurance premiums have surged — especially in Florida. Here are 8 legitimate ways to reduce your premium without cutting the coverage that matters.

children.text: Why premiums keep rising

Homeowner's insurance premiums have increased 20-40% in many markets over the past three years, with Florida seeing some of the steepest increases due to hurricane risk, litigation trends, and reinsurance costs. Several major insurers have withdrawn from the Florida market entirely. This makes finding legitimate savings more important than ever.
Upgrades that lower your premium
Roof upgrades.

Your roof material and age are among the biggest factors in your insurance premium, especially in Florida. Impact-resistant shingles or metal roofing can reduce your windstorm premium by 20-30%. A new roof — regardless of material — typically reduces your premium versus a roof over 15 years old.
Hurricane shutters or impact glass.

In Florida, having wind mitigation features verified by a licensed inspector can result in significant credits. Get a wind mitigation inspection ($150) — the premium savings often pay for it in the first month.
Home security systems.
A monitored alarm system typically reduces your premium by 5-15%. Smart locks, cameras, and water leak detectors are also credited by some carriers.
Updated electrical, plumbing, and HVAC.
Homes with updated systems are lower risk. Tell your insurer when you replace major systems — it may reduce your premium or prevent a non-renewal.
Policy and shopping strategies
Raise your deductible.
Moving from a $1,000 to a $2,500 deductible can reduce your premium by 10-20%. Only do this if you have the cash reserve to cover the higher deductible if you need to file a claim.
Bundle with auto.
Most carriers offer a 5-15% discount for bundling home and auto. Run the numbers — bundling isn't always the cheapest option, but often is.
Shop every 2-3 years.

Loyalty doesn't pay in insurance. Rates vary dramatically between carriers for identical coverage. An independent insurance agent (not a captive agent for one company) can quote multiple carriers simultaneously.
Review your coverage amounts annually.

Make sure you're insuring for replacement cost, not market value. In Florida, construction costs have risen significantly — your coverage limit should reflect current rebuild costs, not what you paid for the home.
Document for faster claims

The best insurance strategy includes thorough documentation. A complete home inventory with photos and model numbers means faster claim settlement and less dispute. Steadwell's asset tracker and document vault keep this organized and cloud-backed automatically.

title: The Landlord's Guide to Property Maintenance Tracking
description: Managing maintenance across rental properties is where landlords lose money and tenants. Here's a system for tracking repairs, documentation, and vendor relationships at scale.

children.text: Why maintenance tracking matters more for landlords

As a homeowner, a maintenance failure inconveniences you. As a landlord, it exposes you to liability, violates habitability standards, and can result in rent withholding or lease termination. Florida law requires landlords to maintain rental properties in a condition that complies with applicable building, housing, and health codes — and to respond to written repair requests within 7 days for non-emergency items.
What to track for each property
System ages and expected replacement dates.

Every property's HVAC, water heater, roof, and major appliances should be documented with age and expected replacement window. This lets you budget replacements into your cash flow projections rather than absorbing them as surprises.
All tenant repair requests.

Every repair request should be documented in writing — when it was received, what the issue was, when you responded, what action was taken, and when it was resolved. This documentation is your protection in a dispute.
Vendor relationships and costs.

Track which contractors you use for each property, their contact information, typical response time, and cost per service type. Over time this becomes a vendor performance record that guides future hiring.
Service history.

A complete service log for each property — HVAC services, pest control, plumbing repairs, appliance work — demonstrates that you maintain the property properly. This matters for insurance claims, security deposit disputes, and potential litigation.
Building your vendor network

Landlords who get great service from contractors aren't luckier than those who don't — they're better customers. Pay invoices the same day. Give clear access instructions. Don't call for price quotes when you're not ready to proceed. Contractors who know you're reliable will pick up your calls and prioritize your work.
The preventive maintenance schedule

For each rental property, establish an annual preventive maintenance schedule: HVAC service (twice yearly in Florida), pest control quarterly, gutter cleaning twice yearly, dryer vent cleaning annually, and smoke detector testing at every lease renewal. These are small costs that prevent large ones and protect you from habitability claims.

Steadwell Pro supports up to 3 properties with shared access — useful for property managers or co-owners who need to see the same home's history. Each property maintains its own asset list, maintenance log, expense tracker, and document vault independently.

title: How to Prepare Your Home for Sale: The Maintenance Checklist
description: Homes with documented maintenance histories sell faster and for more money. Here's exactly what to fix, document, and disclose before you list.

children.text: Why maintenance history matters to buyers

In a competitive market, buyers are choosing between homes that look similar on the surface. A well-documented maintenance history — showing regular HVAC service, roof inspections, and system upgrades — signals that the home has been cared for and reduces buyer anxiety about hidden problems. Homes with maintenance records move faster and with fewer negotiation concessions.
12 months before listing
Address deferred maintenance.
Make a list of every repair you've been putting off and get it done. Buyers and their inspectors will find deferred maintenance. Doing it yourself costs less and lets you control the narrative.
Service major systems.
Schedule HVAC service, water heater flush, and a roof inspection. Keep the service records — they become part of your disclosure package.
Update anything near end of life.
If your water heater is 10 years old or your HVAC is 15, consider replacing proactively. A new water heater costs $1,200 installed. A buyer credit demanded after inspection might be $2,000-3,000.
60-90 days before listing
Get a pre-listing inspection.
Know what's in your home before the buyer's inspector does. This eliminates surprises, lets you make repairs on your schedule, and gives you the option to price accordingly or disclose and adjust.
Address curb appeal.
First impressions happen before buyers walk in. Fresh paint, clean landscaping, a power-washed driveway, and a functional front door set expectations for the rest of the home.
Document everything you've done.
Compile service records, receipts, permits, and warranties for all improvements. This package goes to your realtor and eventually to the buyer's agent.
At listing
Prepare your disclosure honestly.
Disclosing known issues protects you legally and builds buyer trust. Failing to disclose material defects is the most common source of post-closing litigation.
Transfer warranties where possible.
Roof warranties, appliance warranties, and home warranties are sometimes transferable. Check each one — this is a selling point.
Leave your home history for the buyer.

A Steadwell export of your property's asset list, maintenance log, and document vault is one of the most useful things you can leave the next owner. It's a differentiator that most sellers don't think to offer.

title: What Is a Home Health Score — and Why Does It Matter?
description: A home health score gives you a single number that reflects the overall condition of your home's systems. Here's what goes into it and how to improve yours.

children.text: The problem with home maintenance visibility

Most homeowners have no reliable way to know whether their home is in good shape or quietly deteriorating. Individual tasks get done or don't, systems age, maintenance falls behind — but there's no single view of overall home condition. A health score fixes that.
What goes into a home health score

A well-designed home health score evaluates multiple dimensions of your home's condition simultaneously. Steadwell's health score considers: the age and remaining lifespan of major systems (HVAC, water heater, roof, appliances), the completeness of your maintenance history, whether scheduled tasks are current or overdue, and the documentation coverage of your assets. Each factor is weighted by its impact on home value and safety.
Why a single number is useful

Complex systems become manageable when reduced to a meaningful summary. A health score of 82/100 tells you at a glance that your home is in good shape with room for improvement — and drilling down shows you exactly which systems are pulling the score down. It's the same reason credit scores changed how people think about their finances: visibility drives behavior.
How to improve your score
Complete overdue maintenance.
Every overdue task reduces your score. Checking off HVAC service, gutter cleaning, or dryer vent cleaning has an immediate impact.
Document your assets.
A system that's undocumented can't be tracked. Adding appliances, their ages, and their service history improves both your score and your actual knowledge of your home.
Stay ahead of replacements.
Systems approaching end of life reduce your score and represent real risk. The score surfaces these before they become emergencies.
Health score vs. home inspection

A home inspection is a point-in-time assessment. A health score is ongoing — it updates as you complete tasks, add assets, and document your home. The inspection tells you where your home stood on one day; the health score tells you where it stands right now.

title: The Hidden Costs of Homeownership Nobody Talks About
description: The mortgage payment is just the beginning. Here are the costs of homeownership that catch first-time buyers off guard — with real numbers.

children.text: What the mortgage calculator doesn't show you

When most people calculate the cost of homeownership, they add up mortgage payment, property taxes, and homeowner's insurance. But that number — the one the bank qualifies you on — leaves out a significant category of costs that renters don't pay. Understanding the full picture before you buy prevents financial stress after you close.
The costs renters never pay
Maintenance and repairs:
The standard estimate is 1-3% of home value annually. On a $350,000 home, that's $3,500-10,500 per year that doesn't appear anywhere in a mortgage payment.
HOA fees:

If you're buying in a community with an HOA, fees range from $100-800/month depending on amenities and community type. In Florida, condo HOA fees have increased significantly following new requirements for reserve funding after the Surfside collapse.
Utilities:

Renters in many markets pay utilities, but the cost as a homeowner — particularly for a larger space — is often higher than expected. Florida homeowners pay an average of $140-200/month in electricity alone, more in summer.
Lawn and landscaping:
In Florida, lawn care is a year-round expense. Professional service runs $100-300/month depending on lot size. DIY requires equipment investment and time.
Pest control:
In Florida this is non-negotiable. Termites, ants, and roaches require regular treatment. Annual contracts run $400-800/year; termite bonds are an additional $200-400/year.
Property tax increases:

Florida's homestead exemption caps assessment increases at 3% per year for primary residents. But new buyers pay taxes on the assessed value at purchase — which may be significantly higher than what the previous owner paid.
The costs that blindside most buyers
Closing costs:
2-5% of purchase price, typically $7,000-20,000 on a Florida home. Some are negotiable, some aren't — understand what you're paying before signing.
Moving expenses:
$1,500-5,000 for local moves, more for long-distance. Often underestimated.
Immediate improvements:
Most buyers underestimate how much they'll spend in the first 6 months — paint, fixtures, appliances, landscaping. Budget $5,000-15,000 for a realistic move-in fund beyond your down payment.
The total cost of ownership calculation

Add your monthly mortgage payment, property taxes, insurance, HOA fees, utilities, and maintenance reserve. Compare that number honestly to what you'd pay in rent for equivalent space. For many buyers in current markets, renting is cheaper in the short term — but homeownership builds equity that renting doesn't. Know the real number before you decide.

title: Home Maintenance Myths That Are Costing You Money
description: Some of the most common home maintenance advice is wrong — and following it can cost you thousands. Here's what's actually true.

children.text: Myth 1: If it ain't broke, don't fix it

This is the most expensive myth in homeownership. HVAC systems, water heaters, and roofs don't announce their failure in advance — they work fine until they don't. The systems that receive preventive maintenance fail less often, last longer, and when they do fail, fail in less catastrophic ways. A water heater that's flushed annually and has its anode rod replaced lasts 12-15 years. One that's ignored lasts 8-10 and often fails by flooding instead of just losing efficiency.
Myth 2: You should wait for a home inspection to find problems

Home inspections find visible problems at a moment in time. They don't tell you a water heater has 18 months left, that the HVAC hasn't been serviced in 6 years, or that the roof is showing early signs of granule loss. Proactive monitoring between inspections — knowing your system ages, tracking maintenance, looking at your home with attention — catches far more than periodic inspections.
Myth 3: Higher-end appliances last longer

Generally false. Professional-grade and luxury appliances often have more complex electronics, specialized parts, and require specialized service. A $2,000 refrigerator doesn't necessarily outlast a $900 one — it's often just harder and more expensive to repair. Brand-name mid-tier appliances from established manufacturers (Whirlpool, GE, LG, Samsung) often have the best combination of reliability and serviceability.
Myth 4: A new home doesn't need maintenance

New construction requires some of the most attentive early maintenance. Concrete cures and settles for years after pouring, causing cracks that need monitoring. Wood framing shrinks and expands as it acclimates. New appliances need their filters and connections checked in the first year. Grading and drainage issues that weren't apparent before landscaping gets established often emerge in years 1-3.
Myth 5: Painting over problems fixes them

Paint covers cosmetic issues. It doesn't address moisture intrusion, wood rot, mold, or structural movement — it hides them, often making them worse by sealing moisture in. Any time you're painting over something that previously required repair, make sure the underlying issue is genuinely resolved, not just concealed.
Myth 6: Your homeowner's insurance covers everything

Homeowner's insurance covers sudden, accidental damage — a tree falls on your roof, a pipe bursts and floods the house. It explicitly excludes maintenance failures, gradual deterioration, and damage from deferred maintenance. If your water heater rusts through from neglect, that's not covered. If a storm damages your roof and the adjuster finds deferred maintenance contributed, coverage may be disputed. Maintenance isn't just good practice — it protects your ability to make a claim.
